content: Inhaled beta-agonist therapy is a cornerstone in the treatment of acute asthma. However, the potential role of intravenous (IV) beta2-agonists in managing severe acute asthma in the emergency department has been explored. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of IV beta2-agonists in this clinical setting. To identify relevant studies, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were sourced from the Cochrane Airways Group Register, which includes systematic searches of databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and CENTRAL, as well as manual searches of 20 respiratory journals. Bibliographies of included studies and existing reviews were also examined. Additionally, primary authors and subject matter experts were contacted to identify eligible studies. The inclusion criteria were limited to RCTs involving patients presenting to the emergency department with acute asthma. These patients were treated with IV selective or nonselective beta2-agonists, compared to placebo, inhaled beta2-agonists, or other standard care. Outcome measures included pulmonary function, vital signs, arterial blood gases, adverse effects, and clinical success. Two independent reviewers screened and selected studies for inclusion, and the methodological quality of the studies was assessed using two scoring systems. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers and verified with corresponding authors. Missing data were either obtained directly from the authors or calculated from the available information in the studies. A random-effects model was used to combine trial data, and results were reported as odds ratios (OR) or weighted mean differences (WMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Out of 746 references initially identified, 55 potentially relevant articles were reviewed, and 15 studies involving a total of 584 patients were included in the analysis. The findings indicated that the use of selective IV beta2-agonists did not provide any significant advantage over comparator treatments. For instance, after 60 minutes, the peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) was lower in the IV beta2-agonist group compared to the inhaled beta2-agonist group, although the difference was not statistically significant (−24.7 L/min; 95% CI −52.3 to 2.9). Heart rate differences between the groups were also negligible (4.5 bpm; 95% CI −4.9 to 14.0). Furthermore, in well-conducted blinded studies, there was no significant difference in autonomic side effects between the treatment groups (OR 2.2; 95% CI 0.9 to 5.7). In conclusion, there is no evidence to support the routine use of IV beta2-agonists in patients with severe acute asthma. The preferred route of administration for these drugs remains inhalation. No specific subgroups were identified in which the IV route would be advantageous.
